newsitem.title: THAILAND: Analysts await key data for signs of Thai turnaround.
newsitem.headline: Analysts await key data for signs of Thai turnaround.

text.p: Thai export and cash balance figures will be closely watched for signs of a turnaround in the slowing economy when the central bank releases monthly data on Thursday, analysts said.
"These two figures are important because it is a matter of confidence which could affect sentiment in the Thai baht," said Chia Woon Khien, an economist of Skaninaviska Enskilda Banken in Singapore.
Most analysts surveyed by Reuters were bearish and forecast that February exports would drop month on month, due to weak demand exacerbated by long holidays in the region.
But the trade deficit was likely to shrink from around 39 billion baht ($1.5 billion) in January due to a sharp drop in imports, they said.

Key monthly data the Bank of Thailand will release on Thursday include figures on the February trade balance and current account balance, and the March balance of payments, money supply, private investment index and manufacturing production index.
Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutche Morgan Grenfell, forecast exports would slide to 110-112 billion baht from a preliminary 115.9 billion in January.
Imports, on the other hand, were likely to plummet to 134-135 billion baht from 154.9 billion seen in January, shrinking the trade gap to 23-24 billion baht, she said.
Other analyst forecasts reflected similar trends.
"The overall picture is not encouraging. The narrower trade deficit (expected in February) will reflect a sharp drop in imports and not improvement in exports," she said.
Any drop in imports would be attributed to a decrease in raw material and capital goods purchases, analysts said.

"The anticipated sharp fall in imports is barely good news because it indicates a drop in raw material and capital goods. This indicates investors' confidence remains shaky and they are reluctant to produce at the same pace," Arporn said.
An analyst from a leading U.S. investment bank said the exports figure would be watched closely as the country's growth rate depended on it heavily.
On the Thai cash balance, the government has run a cash deficit of 45 billion baht in the first five months of fiscal 1996/97 (October-September) as revenue collection has barely met targets.
Analysts expected the cash balance in March to turn from a deficit of five billion baht to a surplus on the back of revenue from personal income tax.

"The government has talked a lot about the budget cuts to restore confidence and the market is watching to see how this will translate into figures," said SE Bank's Chia Woon Khien, referring to recent massive spending cuts by the Thai government to narrow the current account deficit.
"During the same period last year, the government enjoyed quite a big surplus. If the cash balance of March remains in deficit despite revenue (from personal income), it won't look good," she said.
Thailand last month revamped the ailing finance sector by ordering financial institutions with bad loans to the depressed property sector to boost provisions for sub-standard assets.
Private economists see Thailand's economic growth slowing to just over five percent this year against 6.7 percent in 1996.
